g.text: 05 / CAPITAL ONE’S DURABILITY QUESTION
Separate software lifespan from failure consequence
Lifespan guides maintenance investment; consequences still determine the required checks.
Short-lived / bounded consequence
Simple and removable.
Explicit scope, owner and retirement condition.
Avoid silently accumulating dependencies.
Long-lived / bounded consequence
Maintainable and owned.
Stable interfaces, documentation and regression checks
appropriate to the continuing responsibility.
Short-lived / high consequence
Constrained and checked.
Access, numerical evidence and execution boundaries
remain essential even in a temporary tool.
Long-lived / high consequence
Operated and verified.
Explicit controls, recovery and continuing validation;
reassess as users and responsibilities grow.
Capital One’s conceptual discussion establishes neither deployed disposable software nor zero replacement cost.
Cheap regeneration does not reduce an error’s consequence. Growing use should trigger an explicit maintenance decision.
Sources: Capital One, Sonar and Two Sigma accounts. Qualitative judgment aid; specific checks depend on the workflow.
